title: Growth and IT Leadership: A Practical First 90 Days
excerpt: A first-90-days plan for growth and IT leadership: map the journey, establish a baseline, fix a bottleneck and build accountable operating routines.
body:
A new growth leader can inherit campaigns that appear efficient, a CRM that nobody fully trusts and an operations team already stretched by the existing enquiry volume.

The easiest visible move is to change the campaign plan. The more useful first question is where the organisation loses information, ownership or momentum between acquisition and delivery.

My work has moved across field distribution, real estate marketing and healthcare growth, and my current role is Head of Growth & IT at ANKURAM IVF. That combination has taught me to see acquisition, operating processes and technology as connected responsibilities.

The first 90 days should establish enough shared understanding to make focused improvements and measure them honestly. The plan below is a proposed leadership approach, not a claim that every organisation can transform its performance within three months.

## Agree the mandate before announcing the roadmap

“Own growth” can mean very different things to a founder, a sales manager and an IT team.

I would begin by agreeing the decisions the role owns, the outcomes it influences and the systems it does not control. Clarify who can change budgets, approve messaging, define CRM stages, assign operational work and accept a software release.

In a healthcare organisation, for example, marketing and growth systems should support enquiry progression while clinical and billing systems retain their designated authority. A broader job title does not remove professional or system boundaries.

The mandate should also name the immediate business constraint. Is the organisation struggling to generate relevant demand, respond to it, convert it into appointments or measure what is already happening? Those problems require different first moves.

## Days 1–15: trace the real operating journey

I would follow representative enquiries from their origin through the current process. Review the records with the people responsible for each stage rather than relying only on a management presentation.

The objective is to understand what happens in ordinary work: how an enquiry arrives, when it appears in the CRM, who receives it, how follow-up is recorded and where the next team sees the outcome.

Include exceptions. A late import, a repeat enquiry, an unavailable owner and an appointment that moves between dates often reveal more about the system than the perfect-path demonstration.

Alongside this, map the tools and accounts that support the journey. Identify the owner of each important configuration and integration. Access to a system should be based on the role's authorised responsibilities; an inventory does not require copying all data or credentials into a new document.

The output is a short operating map with documented handoffs, known failure points and open questions.

## Days 16–30: establish a baseline people can reproduce

A baseline is useful only if another person can explain how it was calculated.

I would agree the definitions of a valid enquiry, a relevant conversation, a booking and the appropriate confirmed downstream outcome. Specify the source, cohort window and owner of each measure.

Separate historical gaps from current operating failures. A backlog of unmatched old records may require a reconciliation project, while today's unassigned enquiries require immediate operational attention. Combining both into a single “CRM cleanup” task makes prioritisation harder.

By day 30, I would aim to have three practical outputs:

- A shared journey and system-ownership map.
- A small baseline report with definitions and known limitations.
- A ranked list of problems with evidence, likely impact and an accountable owner.

The date is a planning boundary, not a reason to present incomplete numbers as final. Where evidence is missing, the baseline should say so.

## Prioritise by the cost of the bottleneck

I would evaluate candidate improvements through four questions: how often the problem occurs, how much useful work it blocks, how confident we are about its cause and how safely we can change it.

This avoids prioritising only what is technically interesting or easy to demonstrate.

For example, a new management interface may be attractive, but correcting a broken assignment rule could help the team immediately. Conversely, a reporting discrepancy that affects major budget decisions may deserve attention even when it does not interrupt today's work.

Record dependencies. A new attribution dashboard depends on reliable source relationships; a new appointment campaign depends on available capacity. A roadmap that ignores those dependencies can deliver features without delivering a usable operating improvement.

## Days 31–60: improve one important journey

I would choose a bounded intervention with an observable outcome. Examples include reducing unassigned enquiries, making callbacks visible to managers or improving the accuracy of a particular source-to-CRM relationship.

The intervention should have a hypothesis and an acceptance test. “Connect the tools” is an implementation task. “Every valid enquiry in the test cohort receives an accountable owner, and exceptions are visible” is an outcome the team can review.

Avoid changing too many variables at once when the aim is to learn what caused an improvement. If the audience, creative, staffing and CRM stages all change together, a better result may be welcome but difficult to explain.

I would run the improvement with the team doing the work, inspect representative records and document what failed. AI-assisted implementation or automation can accelerate parts of the work, but neither removes the need to verify the full journey.

## Give each decision a responsible owner

Cross-functional work slows down when everyone is consulted but nobody is accountable.

A lightweight ownership table can prevent that:

| Decision | Accountable function | Essential input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Campaign proposition and spend | Growth or marketing owner | Business priorities, capacity and performance evidence |
| Enquiry assignment and response coverage | Operations or sales owner | Workload, availability and service standards |
| CRM definition or field change | Designated CRM/process owner | Reporting needs and frontline use |
| Clinical content approval | Appropriate clinical authority | Editorial clarity and current evidence |
| Software release acceptance | Named product/business owner | Technical checks and user-journey evidence |

Actual titles will differ. The purpose is to make the decision route clear enough that routine work does not wait for informal escalation every time.

## Days 61–90: prove the result and make it repeatable

The final month should examine whether the improvement holds beyond the first successful test.

Compare against the agreed baseline using equivalent definitions and observation windows. Inspect whether the change shifted work to another team, increased exceptions elsewhere or depends on one person manually rescuing it.

For an automation, review recovery and unresolved queues. For a campaign change, review mature-cohort quality and operating capacity. For a software release, confirm that intended users can complete the task and that support knows how to handle ordinary problems.

Then turn the working practice into a manageable process: a short guide, an owner, a review cadence and a clear escalation route. A result that disappears when the project lead is unavailable has not yet become an organisational capability.

## Keep the leadership review small and specific

I would use a weekly review to connect acquisition performance, operating exceptions, data health and the current improvement effort.

The discussion should finish with a limited set of decisions. Each should record the evidence, action, owner and review date. The following week begins by checking what happened, rather than introducing a completely new list of priorities. The [RevOps dashboard design article](/blogs/revops-dashboard-metrics-decisions) develops this metric-to-decision connection in more detail.

This cadence also reveals when the plan needs to change. If the suspected bottleneck was wrong, update the diagnosis. Protecting an original roadmap is less useful than responding to better evidence.

Senior stakeholders need a clear distinction between verified results, plausible explanations and work still awaiting acceptance. That clarity supports trust even when an experiment does not deliver the hoped-for improvement.

## Present a 90-day review that helps the next decision

The review should answer five questions: what was happening at the start, what changed, what evidence supports the result, what remains uncertain and what should happen next.

I would include the operating map, the agreed metric definitions, the tested improvement, its limitations and the next set of dependencies. Avoid claiming organisation-wide transformation from one successful workflow or a short period of better campaign numbers.

For hiring teams, this is also a useful way to assess a growth and IT candidate. Ask them to explain a handoff, a failed assumption, an acceptance test and the limits of a reported result. Those answers reveal how they work across functions more clearly than a list of platforms alone.

Growth leadership becomes valuable when the organisation can acquire demand, act on it and understand the result with increasing confidence. The first 90 days should build the habits and evidence that make that possible.
